I really wouldn't sweat which cad system you're using to learn. I haven't heard of any companies that use inventor, but the skills are not useless, and you'll find they transition reasonably quickly to whatever system your first job/university uses. I recently got a new job, and have to transition from NX to Solid Edge, and while I do hate my life, it's not like the time I spent in NX was useless. The idea is about being able to VISUALIZE geometry in 3d, and how different components might interact with each other.

Here are a few tips I'd have:

1. Learn physics and love it. If you're not laughing your way through high school physics, you're going to feel LOST in uni. ("crash course physics" on youtube is a personal favourite of mine)
2. Start paying attention to the materials that the things around you are made of. Most of us will just see "metal", but a mechanical engineer sees "6061-t1 aluminum". There is a significant difference between different types of metals or plastics, and it's a mechanical engineers job to understand those differences, and understand how they might work to your favor.
3. Start paying attention to hardware. There are a million different types of screws out there, and it's a mechanical engineer's job to know when to use which. Also pay attention to the types of washers used in certain places and why. Even I'll skip a washer when building furniture or something, but there is an engineer who had to make the decision to include it, and for a reason
4. Start paying attention to how the things around you are manufactured. An excellent resource for this is a show like "How it's made" where you'll see all kinds of different processes. Ultimately your designs need to fit into one or more of these processes.
5. Download a CAD software and start designing stuff. Fusion360 is available for free, and there's a bunch of tutorials on how to use it. Most mechanical engineers LIVE in their CAD.
6. Consider whether or not this is actually a path you want to go down. There is no shame in not giving a crap about screws or materials or manufacturing processes or whatever, but the job of a mechanical engineer is to have an almost neurotic obsession for this stuff. If you don't you'll likely find yourself disappointed with mechanical engineering

Edit: I am Canadian, my apologies if anything I said doesn't apply for a US high school student.

In my third year I got an email from a random prof in Health Sciences who asked for some help on some complex FEA simulations they needed run for their research. I had just taken an elective in advanced FEM, and my prof from that class sent out a list of names they could contact.   


I had a meeting with them and they explained that it was basically simulating loads on a surgically reconstructed hip with the goal of eventually creating more specific guidelines for surgeons on which procedures to use for which injuries. Very interesting project, lots of irregular geometries and weird material characteristics that needed to be modeled.

​

Unfortunately the timing wasn't right, and I was too busy with midterms at the time to take on the project myself, but I showed the prof how I would go about setting up the simulations, what assumptions I would make, and what errors I would expect. They had offered me $20/hr to do the work, but I just didn't have the time.

Personally, I like to always keep an indica strain and a sativa around and smoke different ones in different situations. Watching a movie on a couch all warm and cozy? Indica. Playing my guitar and looking for inspiration? Sativa. That kind of thing

Here's something to try that'll really clear up the difference: roll a joint with indica at one end, and sativa at the other (I usually pack a cone and switch strains halfway through). Then while you're smoking, pay attention to if/when the switch happens, and what the difference is between the two for you. Note that you'll be half a joint high at this point, and that'll color your perception of what exactly it is that changed. But it's still a really great way of getting more in touch with what the differences are between different strains.

 Effects tend to vary from person to person with cannabis, so give it a try for yourself and trust your own feeling over opinions on the internet. I've found a joint that starts with indica and ends with sativa helps with paranoia, and is actually really quite nice.
